transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

I guess I’m here because I can’t seem to stop worrying once something gets into my head. It sounds a little silly when I say it out loud, but it’s like… if I start thinking about my mother getting up at night, whether she might fall or need something, I just keep turning it over and over. And then it shifts to something at work, like a grant report I’m responsible for, or whether I missed some detail in the collections or forgot to follow up on something.

I’m a librarian—well, media collections specialist—so I’m used to being organized, making lists, keeping track of things. But lately, or maybe not just lately, the lists don’t really settle it. I’ll write things down, check them, try to redirect myself, tell myself I’ve done what I can, but my mind just won’t shelve the worry, if that makes sense. It keeps pulling the same thing back out again. That’s really why I came in.
Do you ever have thoughts that bother you, that you wish you could stop thinking about, even though you know they might not make much sense?

Yes… yes, that’s actually a lot of what I mean. It’s not that the thoughts are bizarre exactly, they’re usually about real things—my mother getting up at night, whether she might need me, or something at work like a grant report or a detail I might have missed in the collections. But the way they get stuck feels unreasonable.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you’ve checked the email, you’ve done what you can,” and I’ll even try to move on to another task, but it’s like my mind keeps pulling the same worry back off the shelf. I wish I could just… put it away. I know making one more list or replaying it again probably isn’t helping, but once it starts, I have a very hard time stopping it.
When these worries come up, do you feel driven to do something, like checking things repeatedly, making lists, or going over details in your mind to try to feel more certain or reduce your anxiety?

Yes, I do—though it’s not always like I’m physically getting up and checking a lock or something. A lot of it is mental. Once the worry starts, I feel this pull to do something with it, like if I can just make one more list, or review the email one more time, or go back over the steps in my head, then maybe I’ll finally feel sure.

With my mother, for example, I’ll think about whether she might get up during the night and need something, or whether I’ve thought through everything that could happen. And with work, if it’s a grant report or some detail in the collection records, I’ll keep mentally circling it—did I miss something, did I follow up, did I write it down clearly enough. I can tell myself I’ve already checked, and I’ll try to redirect myself, but it doesn’t really stay put. It’s like I can’t shelve it in my mind. I keep taking the worry back out, even when I know I’m not getting anywhere new.
Do these recurring worries and the need to mentally review things interfere with your ability to get things done during the day, or cause you a lot of distress?

Yes. I wish I could say it was just unpleasant but contained, but it has started spilling into the day in ways I’m really embarrassed by.

At the library, I’ve been missing small details—nothing catastrophic, but the kind of small-but-important things I normally pride myself on catching. A note in a record, a follow-up that should have been clearer, little pieces that affect other people’s work. And because my job is so much about organization and accuracy, even one missed detail feels like proof that I’m not keeping things together.

The bigger thing was a grant presentation. I had prepared, I really had, but when it came time to lead part of it, I just froze. My mind got stuck on whether I had forgotten something or whether there was a flaw in what I was about to say, and I couldn’t move through it smoothly. I ended up having to hand off parts of it to someone else, which is not like me at all.

And since then I keep thinking, if I can’t reliably lead something like that, can I really keep leading my team well? So yes, it causes distress, but it’s also starting to affect how I function at work, and that scares me.

Are there times when these intrusive worries feel completely unwanted, and you struggle with them because you know they don’t make sense, but you still can’t seem to control them no matter how hard you try?

Yes. That’s exactly it. It’s not that I believe the worry is always logical at the level it takes over—I can usually see that I’ve already done what I can. I’ll think, “You made the list, you checked the report, you wrote down the follow-up,” or with my mother, “She’s okay right now, you don’t need to keep running through every possible thing that could happen tonight.” But knowing that doesn’t seem to make it stop.

It’s like once a worry gets started, I can’t shelve it. And I keep using that word because that’s how it feels to me, being a librarian—I should be able to put it in its place and move on. But instead it keeps sliding back out. A grant report, something I might have missed at work, my mother getting up in the night… I can try to redirect myself, I can make another list, I can tell myself I’m being repetitive, but it doesn’t give me the relief I’m looking for. It just keeps looping.

And yes, it feels unwanted. I don’t sit down and choose to spend my time this way. I really want to stop, especially when I can tell I’m not solving anything new. But no matter how hard I try to push it aside or reason with myself, it keeps coming back.

When these worries come back, do you feel you have to perform specific mental acts or behaviors in a certain way to try to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening, even if you know it might be excessive?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as having to do things in a very specific way, like a ritual with exact steps. It’s more… I get pulled into trying to settle the worry somehow, and I’ll review things or make notes or go back over something in my mind, but I don’t know that it has a particular order or rule to it.

I mean, sometimes it feels like, “If I just think this through one more time, I’ll feel better,” but it isn’t like I have to count or repeat a phrase or check something a certain number of times. It’s more that I’m trying to get certainty, I suppose. Like with work, I might reread or mentally replay what I did, but not because I believe some exact action will prevent something terrible. It’s more that I’m uncomfortable leaving it alone.

So… I don’t know. I do feel driven to keep reviewing, but I wouldn’t say there’s a specific mental act that has to be performed in a certain way. If that distinction makes sense.
Can you describe what happens when these worries come into your mind? Do they feel like thoughts you don’t want and try to resist, even though they keep coming back despite your efforts?

Yes… they do feel unwanted. Not in the sense that I’m choosing to sit down and think through them carefully, like normal problem-solving. It’s more like they arrive and then attach themselves to me.

For example, if I think about my mother getting up at night, it doesn’t just come and go. I’ll start wondering whether something could happen, whether I should have anticipated something, whether I missed some small sign. And even if I tell myself, “You’ve already thought about this, you’ve already done what you can,” it keeps circling back.

It’s the same with work. A grant report, or whether I missed a detail in something at the library — once that thought gets in, I can’t seem to shelve it. I keep using that word because that’s exactly how it feels. I want to put it away, in the right place, and move on with the rest of my day. But it doesn’t stay there. It slides back out, and then I’m making another list, or mentally reviewing what I did, or trying to reassure myself that I didn’t overlook something.

And I do try to resist it. I’ll redirect myself, tell myself I’m being repetitive, try to focus on something else. But it’s like my mind doesn’t accept the answer. No matter how many lists I make, or how many times I tell myself I’ve already checked or already thought it through, the worry comes back anyway. That’s really why I came in — not because I never worry, but because once a worry starts, I can’t seem to stop it.

When you have these unwanted thoughts, do you feel you must perform some kind of mental action—like counting, repeating words silently, or going over something in a specific way—to try to make the thought go away or prevent something bad from happening?

No, I don’t think so—not in that exact way. I don’t count, or repeat words silently, or have a set phrase I have to say to myself. And I don’t think there’s a particular sequence, like if I don’t do it the right way something bad will happen.

What I do is more like… I keep circling the issue. I’ll go over what I did, or what I might need to do, or whether I missed something, but it doesn’t feel like a formal mental ritual. It’s more that I’m trying to feel settled, and I can’t quite get there. So I might review a conversation in my head, or think through a task again, or make another note, but it’s not “I must repeat this sentence three times” or anything like that.

I suppose the closest thing is that I’m looking for reassurance from my own mind, if that makes sense. Like I want my brain to say, “Yes, that’s enough, you can stop now.” But it rarely does. Still, I wouldn’t say I’m performing a specific mental action to prevent something bad from happening. It’s more a general, uncomfortable need to keep checking the worry from different angles.
Do you ever feel that you need to neutralize these worries by thinking about something else, or by trying to replace them with more positive or reassuring thoughts?

I think I do try to reassure myself, yes, but I’m not sure I’d call it neutralizing in a deliberate way. It’s less like, “I must think a positive thought now to cancel this out,” and more like I’m constantly trying to redirect myself or talk myself down.

Like if the worry is about my mother getting up at night, I’ll tell myself, “You’ve thought about this, there’s nothing else to do right now,” and I’ll try to move on. Or with a grant report or something at work, I might make a list, or check what I wrote down, or remind myself that I handled it. But the problem is that it doesn’t really stay settled. Once the worry starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. That’s actually a good way to put it because I work with collections, and it feels like I’m trying to put the thought back where it belongs, but it keeps slipping out again.

So I’ll try to think of something reassuring, or focus on another task, or tell myself I’m being repetitive, but no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself, it keeps coming back. That’s really what brought me in — not that I have some exact thought I use to cancel it, but that I can’t seem to stop the worry once it gets going.

Do you ever do anything—either in your mind or physically—that you feel you must complete in order to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce your anxiety, even if it doesn’t logically connect to the worry itself?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re describing, where there’s something I feel I have to complete or else something bad will happen. I don’t have a behavior that feels unrelated but mandatory, like touching something a certain number of times or doing a task in a very specific order.

What I do is more connected to the worry itself, I think. If I’m anxious about whether I handled something at work, I might check my notes again, or mentally go back over what I did. If I’m worried about my mother, I’ll think through what I can do or whether there’s something I missed. But that feels tied to the worry, even if it gets excessive and frustrating.

I don’t feel like, “If I don’t do this unrelated thing, something terrible will happen.” It’s more that I’m uncomfortable and unsettled, and I’m trying to get my mind to let go of it. I may make another list, or review something one more time, but it’s not like a rule I have to follow in a particular way. It’s just… I keep trying to reduce the anxiety, and it doesn’t always work.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel that you need to neutralize these worries by thinking about something else, or by trying to replace them with more positive or reassuring thoughts?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is about attempts to mentally neutralize, replace, or reassure oneself against worries; this most directly relates to the difficulty stopping or controlling the worry despite efforts to redirect or reassure myself.

patient.answer:
I think I do try to reassure myself, yes, but I’m not sure I’d call it neutralizing in a deliberate way. It’s less like, “I must think a positive thought now to cancel this out,” and more like I’m constantly trying to redirect myself or talk myself down.

Like if the worry is about my mother getting up at night, I’ll tell myself, “You’ve thought about this, there’s nothing else to do right now,” and I’ll try to move on. Or with a grant report or something at work, I might make a list, or check what I wrote down, or remind myself that I handled it. But the problem is that it doesn’t really stay settled. Once the worry starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. That’s actually a good way to put it because I work with collections, and it feels like I’m trying to put the thought back where it belongs, but it keeps slipping out again.

So I’ll try to think of something reassuring, or focus on another task, or tell myself I’m being repetitive, but no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself, it keeps coming back. That’s really what brought me in — not that I have some exact thought I use to cancel it, but that I can’t seem to stop the worry once it gets going.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsions aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or distress, but not connected in a realistic way to the concern, which would support a diagnosis of OCD (F42) over GAD (F43.20).
doctor.question: Do you ever do anything—either in your mind or physically—that you feel you must complete in order to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce your anxiety, even if it doesn’t logically connect to the worry itself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about compulsive mental or physical rituals performed to prevent harm or reduce anxiety, especially actions that may not logically connect to the worry. The provided symptom profile describes generalized worry and related symptoms, but does not include compulsions or ritualistic behaviors.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not in the way you’re describing, where there’s something I feel I have to complete or else something bad will happen. I don’t have a behavior that feels unrelated but mandatory, like touching something a certain number of times or doing a task in a very specific order.

What I do is more connected to the worry itself, I think. If I’m anxious about whether I handled something at work, I might check my notes again, or mentally go back over what I did. If I’m worried about my mother, I’ll think through what I can do or whether there’s something I missed. But that feels tied to the worry, even if it gets excessive and frustrating.

I don’t feel like, “If I don’t do this unrelated thing, something terrible will happen.” It’s more that I’m uncomfortable and unsettled, and I’m trying to get my mind to let go of it. I may make another list, or review something one more time, but it’s not like a rule I have to follow in a particular way. It’s just… I keep trying to reduce the anxiety, and it doesn’t always work.

inference.note: This turn ruled out key features of F43.20 (Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety), as the patient's symptoms appear to be more persistent, ego-dystonic, and characterized by recurrent intrusive thoughts and mental rituals that are not limited to a stressor or proportional to the stressor. The clinical picture aligns more closely with OCD (F42). No features of a specific phobia or panic attacks were endorsed to suggest other F40-F41 category disorders.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent intrusive thoughts and compulsive mental reviewing behaviors aimed at reducing distress or preventing feared events, which are consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The absence of clear-cut compulsive rituals does not exclude OCD, as mental acts such as reviewing, reassurance-seeking, and thought suppression are well-recognized forms of compulsions. The content of the intrusive thoughts (e.g., concern over missing details at work, fear of harm to a loved one) and the patient’s recognition that the thoughts are excessive or unreasonable further support this diagnosis. Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) was considered but ruled out due to the more obsessive-compulsive nature of the thoughts and the presence of mental compulsions. F06.4 (obsessive-compulsive disorder, organic) was considered only if there was evidence of a neurological or organic basis, which was not present.
